query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 starting from a high-temperature BCC state, slow cooling accentuates elemental segregation that builds localized elastic stresses above a critical level, triggering nucleation of σ and B2 phases during subsequent annealing.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a supersaturated high-temperature BCC state obtained by gas atomization.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to two controlled cooling protocols – slow cooling to maximize elemental segregation versus rapid quenching to minimize it – followed by annealing at 600 °C and 900 °C for 1 hour.
generation.conditions: Applies under ambient pressure and moderate annealing temperatures (600–900 °C); the hypothesis should not apply if the cooling rate is uniform and fast enough to suppress segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional fluctuations and the associated elastic strain fields measured via microhardness and lattice parameter splitting (XRD peak deconvolution) serve as mediators.
generation.mechanism: Elemental segregation during slow cooling leads to local elastic stresses that lower the nucleation barrier for secondary phases, resulting in σ and B2 phase precipitation once a stress threshold is reached.
generation.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will exhibit a higher degree of phase decomposition (as evidenced by the appearance of secondary σ and/or B2 phase peaks in XRD and increased microhardness by ~25% relative to the rapidly quenched baseline), while rapidly quenched samples remain predominantly BCC.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 that retains a single BCC phase with minimal segregation.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected only when cooling allows sufficient diffusion for elemental partitioning; extremely rapid cooling or post-cooling homogenization anneals should not exhibit the secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative thresholds for elastic strain and segregation levels may vary; microstructural characterization resolution might limit detection of subtle phase fractions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform the two cooling protocols followed by identical annealing and compare phase fractions via XRD, SEM/EDS mapping, and microhardness measurements. Additionally, measure local lattice misfits with high-resolution TEM or synchrotron XRD.
measurements: XRD peak splitting and phase identification
EDS elemental mapping to quantify segregation
Microhardness tests comparing values between protocols
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If slow-cooled samples do not show significantly higher elemental segregation, local elastic strain indicators, or secondary phase nucleation compared to rapidly quenched samples under identical annealing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 demonstrates the results of the microhardness test. In initial state, the powder has higher microhardness than cast alloy (760 HV). Despite the fact that no microstructural changes were observed after annealing at 600 °C (Figure 3), microhardness of the powder and L-PBF sample annealed at 600 °C grows by about 25% compared to that in the initial state. This hardness rise may be caused by a growth of elastic stresses between the several BCC solid solutions due to increasing element segregation. After annealing at 900 °C microhardness slightly decreases but remains higher than that in the initial state. From one hand, the decomposition of the solid solution results in stress relaxation and hardness decrease, from other the precipitation of hard and homogeneously distributed σ-phase holds the hardness on a high level (about 850 HV). The powder and L-PBF sample annealed at 900 °C have similar hardness despite the difference in precipitates morphology (Figure 3). papers.system: FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 high‐entropy alloy (HEA) processed by gas atomization, L-PBF, and microplasma spraying
papers.approach: Experimental investigation using XRD, SEM, EDS, DTA, and microhardness measurements on as‐atomized powders and annealed samples
papers.findings: The as-atomized powder crystallized into a supersaturated BCC (or B2-like) structure; annealing at 600 °C increased hardness (likely due to elastic stresses from progressive elemental segregation) and at 900 °C partial decomposition of the BCC solid solution occurred with formation of sigma and B2 phases
papers.mechanism: Elemental segregation during cooling/thermal exposure leads to local elastic stress build-up that, once a threshold is reached, triggers phase decomposition (e.g. sigma precipitation) via interfacial and lattice distortions

papers.title: Orientation Relationships in Al0.7CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy
papers.system: Al0.7CoCrFeNi cast HEA starting in the BCC phase that partially transforms to FCC
papers.approach: Microstructural characterization via EBSD, SEM, and TEM to track nucleation, growth, and crystallographic orientation during BCC to FCC transformation
papers.findings: The transformation from BCC to FCC occurs by a shear mechanism with a dominant Pitsch orientation relationship; the process is influenced by atomic size differences and local composition inhomogeneities as well as the presence of an ordered B2 phase
papers.mechanism: The nucleation of the FCC phase within the parent BCC matrix is primarily governed by shear transformations modulated by lattice distortions induced by local segregation and ordering (B2)

papers.title: Phase transformation and strengthening of the gas-atomized FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder during annealing
papers.system: FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA powder subjected to annealing after rapid solidification
papers.approach: Quantitative analysis of microhardness evolution with annealing temperature and determination of activation energies for decomposition and sigma phase formation
papers.findings: The initial stage of solid solution decomposition exhibits a low activation energy (0.65 eV) attributable to quenched vacancies, whereas significant formation of sigma phase occurs after reaching a threshold elastic deformation (around 1.5% lattice misfit) with an activation energy (~2.6 eV) consistent with self-diffusion in BCC metals
papers.mechanism: Gradual elemental segregation creates localized elastic stresses that eventually overcome a kinetic nucleation barrier, leading to sigma phase precipitations at semicoherent boundaries
